(b) State $A(\eta)$ in terms of $\theta$.

Let  
\[
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i),\qquad \bar T_n=\frac1n S_n,
\]
and let \(\mathcal H=\{\eta:A(\eta)<\infty\}\) be the natural parameter space. The joint density is
\[
L_n(\theta)
=\prod_{i=1}^n h(X_i)\exp\left\{\eta(\theta)S_n-nB(\theta)\right\}.
\]

---

## (a) Sufficient statistic and MLE

By the Fisher–Neyman factorization theorem,
\[
L_n(\theta)=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n h(X_i)\right)\exp\left\{\eta(\theta)S_n-nB(\theta)\right\},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i)}
\]
is sufficient for \(\theta\).

In canonical form, the log-likelihood, up to an additive constant independent of \(\eta\), is
\[
\ell_n(\eta)=\eta S_n-nA(\eta).
\]
Thus the MLE in the natural parameterization is any maximizer of
\[
\eta\mapsto \eta S_n-nA(\eta).
\]
If the maximizer is interior, the score equation is
\[
0=\frac{\partial}{\partial \eta}\ell_n(\eta)
=S_n-nA'(\eta),
\]
so
\[
A'(\widehat \eta)=\bar T_n.
\]
Since \(A'(\eta)=\mathbb E_\eta[T(X)]\), the MLE satisfies
\[
\boxed{\mathbb E_{\widehat\eta}[T(X)]=\bar T_n.}
\]
When \(A'\) is invertible and \(\bar T_n\in A'(\mathcal H)\),
\[
\boxed{\widehat\eta=(A')^{-1}(\bar T_n).}
\]
If \(\eta(\theta)\) is one-to-one, then
\[
\boxed{\widehat\theta=\eta^{-1}\!\left((A')^{-1}(\bar T_n)\right).}
\]

Equivalently, in the original parameterization, an interior MLE satisfies
\[
0=\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\ell_n(\theta)
=\eta'(\theta)S_n-nB'(\theta),
\]
so, when \(\eta'(\theta)\neq 0\),
\[
\boxed{\frac{B'(\widehat\theta)}{\eta'(\widehat\theta)}=\bar T_n.}
\]

If \(\bar T_n\notin A'(\mathcal H)\), then a finite MLE may fail to exist; the supremum may occur at the boundary of the natural parameter space.

---

## (b) Relationship between \(A(\eta)\) and \(B(\theta)\)

Since
\[
p(x\mid \theta)=h(x)\exp\{\eta(\theta)T(x)-B(\theta)\}
\]
must integrate to \(1\),
\[
1=\int h(x)\exp\{\eta(\theta)T(x)-B(\theta)\}\,dx.
\]
Therefore
\[
B(\theta)=\log\int h(x)e^{\eta(\theta)T(x)}\,dx.
\]
But in canonical form,
\[
A(\eta)=\log\int h(x)e^{\eta T(x)}\,dx.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{A(\eta(\theta))=B(\theta).}
\]
If \(\eta(\theta)\) is one-to-one, then
\[
\boxed{A(\eta)=B(\eta^{-1}(\eta)).}
\]

---

## (c) Uniqueness of the MLE

Assume \(T(x)\) is not constant on the support and \(\eta(\theta)\) is one-to-one.

We show \(A\) is strictly convex. On the interior of \(\mathcal H\),
\[
A'(\eta)=\mathbb E_\eta[T(X)]
\]
and
\[
A''(\eta)=\operatorname{Var}_\eta(T(X)).
\]
Because \(T\) is not constant on the support, \(\operatorname{Var}_\eta(T(X))>0\). Thus
\[
A''(\eta)>0,
\]
so \(A\) is strictly convex.

Therefore
\[
\ell_n(\eta)=\eta S_n-nA(\eta)
\]
is strictly concave in \(\eta\). A strictly concave function has at most one maximizer. Hence the MLE \(\widehat\eta\), if it exists, is unique.

Since \(\eta(\theta)\) is one-to-one, uniqueness of \(\widehat\eta\) implies uniqueness of \(\widehat\theta\). Thus, whenever the MLE exists,

\[
\boxed{\text{the MLE is unique.}}
\]

---

For parts (d)–(f), assume \(\eta(\theta)\) is strictly increasing and \(S_n\) has a continuous distribution. Fix a significance level \(0<\alpha<1\).

---

## (d) Most powerful test of \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta=\theta_1\), \(\theta_1>\theta_0\)

Let
\[
\eta_0=\eta(\theta_0),\qquad \eta_1=\eta(\theta_1).
\]
Since \(\eta(\theta)\) is strictly increasing and \(\theta_1>\theta_0\),
\[
\eta_1>\eta_0.
\]

The likelihood ratio is
\[
\frac{L_n(\theta_1)}{L_n(\theta_0)}
=
\exp\left\{(\eta_1-\eta_0)S_n-n[B(\theta_1)-B(\theta_0)]\right\}.
\]
Because \(\eta_1-\eta_0>0\), this likelihood ratio is strictly increasing in \(S_n\).

By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test rejects for large values of \(S_n\). Let \(c_\alpha\) satisfy
\[
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
\]
The continuity assumption guarantees no randomization is needed. Thus the MP test is

\[
\boxed{
\varphi_\alpha(X_1,\dots,X_n)
=
\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_\alpha\}.
}
\]

---

## (e) UMP test of \(H_0:\theta\le \theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta>\theta_0\)

Consider the same test
\[
\varphi_\alpha=\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_\alpha\},
\]
where
\[
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
\]

The family has a monotone likelihood ratio in \(S_n\), because for \(\theta_2>\theta_1\),
\[
\frac{L_n(\theta_2)}{L_n(\theta_1)}
=
\exp\left\{(\eta(\theta_2)-\eta(\theta_1))S_n-n[B(\theta_2)-B(\theta_1)]\right\},
\]
which is increasing in \(S_n\). Therefore, \(S_n\) is stochastically increasing in \(\theta\). Hence, for \(\theta\le \theta_0\),
\[
\mathbb P_\theta(S_n>c_\alpha)
\le
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_\alpha)
=\alpha.
\]
So \(\varphi_\alpha\) has level \(\alpha\) for the composite null \(H_0:\theta\le \theta_0\).

Now fix any \(\theta_1>\theta_0\). For testing the simple hypotheses
\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad
H_1:\theta=\theta_1,
\]
part (d) shows that \(\varphi_\alpha\) is most powerful of size \(\alpha\). Therefore, for any other level-\(\alpha\) test \(\psi\),
\[
\mathbb E_{\theta_1}[\psi]\le \mathbb E_{\theta_1}[\varphi_\alpha].
\]
Since this holds for every \(\theta_1>\theta_0\), \(\varphi_\alpha\) is UMP.

Thus the UMP level-\(\alpha\) test is

\[
\boxed{
\varphi_\alpha(X_1,\dots,X_n)=\mathbf 1\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i)>c_\alpha\right\},
}
\]
where
\[
\boxed{\mathbb P_{\theta_0}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i)>c_\alpha\right)=\alpha.}
\]

This is the Karlin–Rubin theorem for one-parameter exponential families with monotone likelihood ratio.

---

## (f) Existence of a UMP test for \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) vs. \(H_1:\theta\neq\theta_0\)

In general, for a genuine two-sided alternative, there is no nontrivial UMP level-\(\alpha\) test.

Assume the parameter space contains points on both sides of \(\theta_0\). Choose
\[
\theta_+>\theta_0,\qquad \theta_-<\theta_0.
\]

For testing
\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\quad\text{vs.}\quad
H_1:\theta=\theta_+,
\]
the Neyman–Pearson lemma gives the unique most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test
\[
\varphi_+(X)=\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_+\},
\]
where
\[
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n>c_+)=\alpha.
\]

For testing
\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\quad\text{vs.}\quad
H_1:\theta=\theta_-,
\]
because \(\eta(\theta_-)<\eta(\theta_0)\), the likelihood ratio is decreasing in \(S_n\). Therefore the Neyman–Pearson lemma gives the unique most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test
\[
\varphi_-(X)=\mathbf 1\{S_n<c_-\},
\]
where
\[
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}(S_n<c_-)=\alpha.
\]

Suppose a UMP level-\(\alpha\) test \(\varphi\) existed for
\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\quad\text{vs.}\quad
H_1:\theta\neq\theta_0.
\]
Then \(\varphi\) would have to be most powerful against \(\theta_+\), so by uniqueness in the Neyman–Pearson lemma,
\[
\varphi=\varphi_+
\qquad \mathbb P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]
But it would also have to be most powerful against \(\theta_-\), so
\[
\varphi=\varphi_-
\qquad \mathbb P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]
Thus we would need
\[
\mathbf 1\{S_n>c_+\}
=
\mathbf 1\{S_n<c_-\}
\qquad \mathbb P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]
This is impossible for \(0<\alpha<1\). One test rejects in the upper tail, while the other rejects in the lower tail.

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\text{there is no nontrivial UMP level-}\alpha\text{ test for }H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\text{ vs. }H_1:\theta\neq\theta_0.}
\]

Only trivial cases such as \(\alpha=0\) or \(\alpha=1\), or a parameter space with alternatives on only one side of \(\theta_0\), avoid this nonexistence conclusion.
